The art of video editing is a complex process that involves a delicate balance between numerous factors.  A skilled editor combines multiple shots in a way that is aesthetically pleasing and easy to follow, often using techniques such as panning and zooming to draw the viewer's attention to specific parts of the screen.  These techniques are typically applied in a specific order to create a cohesive narrative, with the editor first adding transitions, followed by the insertion of text overlays, before adding effects such as brightness adjustments to enhance the overall mood of the video.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive dataset of 1,000 manually edited videos, along with an accompanying benchmark that tests the ability of AI systems to replicate the editing decisions made by human editors.  The benchmark consists of three tasks: predicting the order in which shots are added to a video, identifying the specific regions of the screen where text overlays should be applied, and determining the level of brightness adjustment needed to enhance the overall mood of the video.  We have developed a state-of-the-art baseline model that performs well on each of these tasks, with accuracy rates of 0.85, 0.82, and 0.81, respectively.  A detailed analysis of the results reveals that the model excels at tasks that rely on a deep understanding of the underlying narrative, but struggles with tasks that require a more nuanced understanding of aesthetics.  We believe that this research has the potential to inspire the development of more sophisticated AI models that can assist human editors in the editing process. This paper introduces the T-product Tensor Enlarger (T-product TE) and derives a novel Chernoff bound for stochastic processes in this context. A Chernoff bound is a type of deviation measure that quantifies the likelihood of stochastic events. Building on the Chernoff bound for scalar random variables, the T-product TE is used to establish a corresponding bound for T-product tensors, which are matrices with a product structure. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this new bound. Notably, the T-product TE offers advantages over existing tensor extensions of the Chernoff bound in several aspects. Firstly, it provides a more general framework for handling stochastic processes, surpassing the capabilities of the T-product tensor enlarger introduced by Li et al. Secondly, the T-product TE can be applied to a broader range of stochastic processes, including those with unbounded and unstructured noise functions, whereas previous approaches were limited to bounded and structured noise. Lastly, the T-product TE can accommodate a wider variety of tensor structures, including those with varying dimensions and ranks, whereas previous extensions were restricted to tensors with specific properties. As a result, the T-product TE offers a more flexible and powerful tool for analyzing stochastic processes. The authors also demonstrate the application of the T-product TE to a specific problem in stochastic adaptive control, where they derive a new bound for the mean-square error and develop a novel adaptive control algorithm. Theoretical analysis and experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this new approach. The T-product TE is expected to have significant practical implications for the design of stochastic control systems. However, the high number of parameters in CNNs poses significant computational challenges for real-time applications, particularly on resource-constrained devices. To mitigate this issue, several filter pruning methods have been proposed, which involve identifying and removing unessential filters from CNNs. This paper presents a novel approach to filter pruning by leveraging the self-similarity matrix (SSM) to evaluate the importance of filters. SSM-based analysis has been successfully applied in image analysis, texture recognition, and computer vision tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first instance of employing SSM in neural network pruning. Our proposed method involves constructing SSM for each filter and subsequently using the SSM's eigenvalues to assess filter significance. We then select the least significant filters for removal. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation on various benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The results demonstrate that our method achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art filter pruning methods, while requiring fewer parameters. Notably, our method is also more efficient and requires less computational resources, making it a promising solution for real-time applications. We introduce WikiGUM, a comprehensive entity linking dataset covering 12 distinct text categories and 14,000 articles in Wikipedia. WikiGUM surpasses existing entity linking datasets in terms of size and scope, providing an extensive range of texts and annotations for 100,000 mentions across various genres. We developed a systematic approach to annotating mentions, incorporating both surface-level and in-depth information, and we highlight the importance of genre-specific features in entity linking through extensive experiments. Our findings demonstrate that models trained on our dataset outperform others in multiple genres, and we believe that WikiGUM sets a new standard for evaluating entity linking techniques in diverse genres and text types. The complete dataset, including annotations and documents, is available for download at https://github.com/EMNLP-WS/WikiGUM. We introduce a new formula for calculating permanent values in specific circulant matrices, characterized by a band structure. This formula allows for the efficient computation of the permanent of circulant determinants within a particular class, namely those with a band of diagonal entries. This novel approach outperforms existing methods in its computational efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the formula to determinants beyond uniform matrices, as long as their structure conforms to the specified pattern. Additionally, we provide a new formula for the permanent of uniform circulant matrices, expressed as a power series of the uniform matrix's permanent. This novel formula is derived from a combinatorial analysis of the alternating group's cycle decomposition. This new formula offers an alternative to the traditional inclusion-exclusion principle and has the potential to be more computationally effective. We also extend our findings to the broader context of the permanent of the monoid of circulant matrices, encompassing both uniform and non-uniform matrices. This generalization is facilitated by utilizing the algebraic properties of the permanent in combination with Burnside's results on group invariants. Finally, we present a combinatorial interpretation of the uniform circulant matrix permanent, demonstrating that it is equivalent to the chromatic polynomial of the uniform graph, a result that is both surprising and intuitive. This interpretation offers a new perspective on the traditional principle of inclusion-exclusion. LADDER works by intentionally corrupting key internal features during the training process, prompting the network to develop stronger boundaries that resist malicious interference. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LADDER on various network architectures and show that it significantly outperforms traditional adversarial training methods, achieving better results in both image classification and semantic segmentation tasks. Cache attacks are a significant threat to confidentiality in modern software, but detecting them has been a difficult task due to the need for sophisticated analysis tools. This challenge is particularly true for production software, where complex dependencies and variable workloads complicate the identification of vulnerable areas. This paper showcases CacheQL's capabilities with two key examples: a micro-benchmark and a real-world application, demonstrating how the tool can effectively quantify and locate sensitive data operations and identify opportunities for exploitation. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach to creating a cache model from micro-benchmarks, which enables the simulation of various workload patterns and helps to pinpoint the most critical vulnerabilities in software. This model can be used to predict the performance impact of cache-side-channel vulnerabilities in real-world scenarios. By providing a straightforward and efficient approach, we make it possible to identify vulnerabilities in large software projects, which would be impractical using traditional methods. This research marks a significant step towards automated cache-side-channel detection and locating in production software. GANs have become a prominent tool in generating synthetic data, but their training process is complicated by a phenomenon known as mode collapse, which occurs when the model fails to produce diverse samples. This issue is difficult to diagnose due to the lack of clear indicators for mode collapse. To address this challenge, we investigate mode collapse by analyzing the Hessian of the generator in a mini-batch setting, where we examine eigenvalue distributions to identify and differentiate collapsed and diverse modes. Our research is grounded in the observation that zero eigenvalues in the Hessian indicate unstable directions that do not contribute to diverse samples. To this end, we propose a new approach to detect mode collapse by analyzing Hessian eigenvalue distributions, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on various datasets, including the CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet datasets. Our results show that this method can accurately identify mode collapse and provide actionable insights for improving GAN training. Additionally, we found that incorporating the Hessian analysis into the training process can mitigate mode collapse and yield better results. Our work provides a foundation for future research on mode detection and combats mode collapse in GANs. However, the lack of interpretable tools hinders the development of reliable models. To address this gap, we introduce the Inverse Survival Model (RSM), a novel framework that facilitates the interpretation of survival models. By leveraging the relationship between survival and classification, RSM converts survival data into a classification format, allowing for the application of established classification explanation techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RSM through experiments on public datasets, showcasing its ability to provide valuable insights into model predictions. Furthermore, RSM's modular design enables seamless integration with other explanation methods, offering a promising foundation for the interpretation of survival models. This paper explores the use of distributed Bayesian inference to track the evolution of latent state variables in complex systems. We examine the simultaneous estimation of the current state and the state transition function, based on noisy sensor measurements and prior knowledge. Our approach is suitable for decentralized systems with limited communication capabilities. We demonstrate that the distributed exchange of local observations and prior updates can converge to the global Bayesian optimal solution. Additionally, we show that the incorporation of a simple, local stability assumption enables efficient computation of this solution in parallel. We validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations. The accompanying video further illustrates the application of this method to track moving objects in real-world scenarios. The related software and additional materials are publicly available for further exploration.

Recent studies have highlighted the vulnerability of neural networks to adversarial examples, which are crafted to deceive neural classifiers. Existing research has primarily focused on generating adversarial examples that exploit semantic attributes. In this study, we introduce a novel method to create unrestricted adversarial examples by targeting non-semantic features. Our approach, which is inspired by the principle of non-deterministic dimensionality, enables the identification of non-semantic feature clusters. We then develop a novel gradient-based method to generate adversarial examples that target these clusters. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method yields adversarial examples with higher success rates and stronger non-semantic properties compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed adversarial examples are non-trivial and possess meaningful visual content. Our findings have important implications for the development of robust neural networks. Aerial surveillance and inspection applications heavily rely on autonomous drones, which are increasingly being used in various settings, including search and rescue operations, and require a reliable detection system to function optimally. To achieve seamless integration with these drones, it's essential to develop a real-time detection system that can identify and track them in real-world scenarios, which is a crucial step towards developing advanced drone capabilities. To address this need, we propose EVPropNet, a cutting-edge AI-based system that can recognize and track drones in mid-air, utilizing a unique combination of 3D convolutional and evolutionary neural networks. Our innovative approach enables accurate and efficient drone detection, even in complex and dynamic environments, outperforming traditional methods. Through extensive testing on a diverse range of real-world datasets, we have demonstrated the exceptional performance and versatility of EVPropNet, which can be easily adapted to different scenarios. Our results show that EVPropNet can achieve impressive accuracy of up to 95.5% and a high frame rate of 30 FPS, even in the most challenging conditions. We believe that EVPropNet has the potential to revolutionize the field of autonomous drone operation and will be an essential tool for developing advanced drone capabilities. Our code and datasets will be made available to the public, enabling others to build upon our work and drive the next generation of drone technology. To this end, we will be open-sourcing our code and datasets, and are excited to collaborate with others to develop the future of drone capabilities. Our research has been accepted for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Engineering Management and is currently undergoing the finalization process. The associated code and datasets will be made available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ashishdmz/EVPropNet. Person re-identification, a critical task in visual computing, has gained significant attention due to its numerous applications. The primary challenge lies in distinguishing between individuals from the same cluster, as this often leads to misclassification. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach, attribute alignment through cluster level prediction (AACLCP), which enhances the model's ability to differentiate between persons. The AACLCP method comprises two key components: a cluster-level classifier and an attribute aligner. The former is designed to predict person clusters, while the latter adjusts feature representations to minimize intra-cluster variation. The AACLCP approach is integrated into our existing re-identification model, which is then evaluated on the Market1501, DukeMTMC-reID, and MSMT17 datasets, resulting in superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Deep reinforcement learning algorithms often struggle with the issue of value function breakdown, which occurs when the estimated Q-values become too large or too small.  This problem is particularly common in deep Q-learning models.  To address this issue, we introduce a new regularization approach that promotes diverse Q-function approximations across multiple models, thereby preventing value function breakdown.  Our proposed method, MaxMin, is an ensemble-based regularization technique that enhances representation diversity by minimizing the minimum and maximizing the maximum Q-values across the ensemble.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of MaxMin in various reinforcement learning tasks, including image-based continuous control and multi-task learning experiments.  Our results show that MaxMin significantly outperforms existing regularization techniques, achieving better results in both sample efficiency and task completion.  Moreover, we find that MaxMin enhances the generalization capabilities of individual models, particularly in multi-task learning settings.  Our research provides a theoretical understanding of the importance of representation diversity in preventing value function breakdown, and we believe that MaxMin can serve as a valuable regularization strategy for various reinforcement learning applications. Federated learning, a technique for distributed model training, has gained significant attention in recent years.  However, its online version faces a unique challenge: how to effectively combine local models trained on non-identical, noisy data sets.  This paper presents a novel framework, MoKaOFLO, that leverages multiple kernel learning to aggregate models from diverse data sets.  By employing a maximum mean discrepancy-based approach, MoKaOFLO can adaptively select the most relevant kernel for data aggregation.  This framework is further enhanced with a dynamic adjustment mechanism to optimize kernel weights, thereby minimizing the impact of noisy data.  Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that MoKaOFLO consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.  Furthermore, MoKaOFLO's adaptability and versatility make it a promising candidate for real-world federated learning applications.  The code for MoKaOFLO is available for public access. Recent studies have highlighted the vulnerability of neural networks to adversarial attacks that inject backdoors, but these attacks have significant limitations. Specifically, they require the adversary to fine-tune the model parameters, a requirement that is impractical in real-world scenarios. To address this, we propose a novel method for injecting backdoors that does not require any modifications to the original model. Instead, we introduce a small number of additional neurons to the neural network, which are trained using a specific adversarial loss function. These new neurons can then be used to misclassify specific target examples, a phenomenon we refer to as Adversarial Neurons. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on a range of benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of attack success rate and stealth. Additionally, we investigate the robustness of our proposed method against defensive techniques and show that it remains highly effective even in the presence of these countermeasures. Feature switches are a widely used software engineering technique that enables developers to toggle the on/off status of specific project features. While feature switches have been primarily employed for debugging purposes, research is lacking on their broader application in open-source software development. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of 1,000 feature switches in 100 open-source projects, examining their relationship with project branches and bug fixes. Our analysis revealed that feature switches are frequently used in conjunction with project merges and that they are more commonly adopted during bug fixing periods. Our study also uncovered instances where feature switches were used incorrectly, highlighting opportunities for the development of more advanced tools to support their effective utilization in software development. By shedding light on the diverse ways feature switches are utilized in open-source projects, our research contributes to the understanding of their underlying technical and developmental aspects. Ultimately, our study aims to inspire the creation of more sophisticated tools to support the development and maintenance of software features. In this context, we demonstrate that the Bethe-Gibbs state can be viewed as a posterior mean with respect to a prior that belongs to an exponential family. Additionally, we show that the Bethe pyramid forms a Donsker-Varadhan type spectral gap bound for Markov chains, and we discuss the potential of our results for statistical inference tasks. Finally, we provide numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of our findings. Few-shot learning, a task involving rapid learning from limited samples, poses significant challenges due to the scarcity of training data.  To address this issue, our proposed method, the Meta-filter, leverages a predictive model that estimates the likelihood of a sample aligning with a specific class, thereby identifying potential misclassifications. Furthermore, our method incorporates a dynamic adjustment mechanism to refine the likelihood estimates, thereby enhancing its predictive capabilities.  Experimental results demonstrate that our method can achieve superior performance in comparison to existing approaches, particularly in scenarios involving few-shot learning.  Notably, our method can also be applied to other meta-learning tasks, such as generalization in image classification and semantic segmentation. The prevalence of pixel defects in display technology has been widely acknowledged.
These pixel defects, commonly known as dead pixels, can significantly impede
the viewer's ability to comprehend visual data, particularly in scenarios where
fine details are crucial. In an effort to address this issue, a novel approach has
been developed to detect dead pixels within images, grounded in the concept of
the Effective Receptive Field. This proposed method draws inspiration from the
key findings of the ERF approach, which effectively leverages convolutional
kernels to concentrate computational resources on specific image areas. In light
of this understanding, a refined ERF metric has been developed, allowing for a
more precise assessment of image regions. This metric serves as the foundation
for a more sophisticated dead pixel detection algorithm, which efficiently
identifies dead pixels within images. This proposed method can be seamlessly
integrated into existing image processing pipelines, enabling applications such
as image denoising, image deblurring, and image enhancement. Notably, the
separation of the dead pixel detection process from the image enhancement process
enables the simultaneous execution of these tasks, thereby facilitating the
development of more advanced image processing techniques. Extensive evaluations
conducted on the LIVE1 dataset have demonstrated the efficacy of this proposed
method, resulting in a 2.5% improvement in image quality over existing state-of-
the-art methods. This proposed method can be accessed at the specified GitHub

The growing adoption of AI-powered edge devices has led to an increased demand for deep neural networks that can be implemented on such edge devices. However, the limited resources on these edge devices make it challenging to achieve high inference precision while meeting the required latency. To overcome this challenge, we propose a highly-efficient edge/cloud collaborative architecture called AppealNet that optimally distributes the inference workload between edge and cloud servers. AppealNet employs a novel AppealNet-Quantizer (ANQ) algorithm that determines which layers of the model should be computed on the edge or cloud, based on the available resources. Our experiments demonstrate that AppealNet significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in terms of inference accuracy and latency. AppealNet is also highly adaptable and efficient, as it can handle complex models with numerous layers and support different hardware configurations. To demonstrate its practicality, we successfully implemented AppealNet on a real-world edge device, achieving a significant reduction in power consumption and memory usage compared to running the entire model on the device. Our results show that AppealNet achieves a high inference accuracy of 99.6% while meeting the required latency of 10ms, which is comparable to the performance of running the entire model on the cloud. AppealNet is now available as an open-source project on GitHub. The quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects occur when a system is repeatedly measured during a process, causing it to stay in an unchanged state or undergo accelerated change. By using a master equation approach, we demonstrate that the rate of change in the system's state depends on the type of interaction and the measurement frequency, leading to unexpected results such as the Zeno effect occurring even with weak measurements, and the anti-Zeno effect being more pronounced at higher interaction strengths. Our findings provide valuable insights for experiments involving the interaction of light with highly excited atoms, and highlight the importance of understanding the measurement process in quantum dynamics. The research also has potential applications in the fields of quantum information and quantum metrology. The proliferation of machine learning in various domains has led to the development of Federated Learning (FL), a technique that enables the training of machine learning models on private data while maintaining client privacy. FL's ability to train models on diverse data sets makes it an attractive solution for scenarios where data homogeneity is low. However, FL's performance is often hindered by the uneven distribution of data, leading to poor model accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that utilizes the client's local data to estimate the global distribution of data, thereby enabling the development of more equitable FL models. Our approach is evaluated on various client-based FL scenarios, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving model accuracy, particularly in scenarios with highly heterogeneous data, and its ability to reduce computational costs. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of FL on model fairness and highlight the need for more rigorous fairness assessments in FL-based systems. To address this, we propose a novel fairness metric and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying and mitigating unfair FL models. Our work contributes to the development of more robust and equitable FL models, and the associated code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/eqFL. In Australia, various health registries are responsible for collecting and maintaining data on specific health conditions. However, these registries are often restricted from sharing sensitive information due to confidentiality and security concerns. To address this issue, we propose a secure federated learning approach that enables the coordination of machine learning tasks across different health registries without revealing sensitive data. Our method involves using secure multi-party computation to compute local gradients and aggregate results securely, while utilizing homomorphic encryption to ensure data protection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting experiments on real-world data from the Australian Organ and Tissue Donation Registry, achieving comparable performance to traditional machine learning models. The proposed technique has broader applications in healthcare, particularly for registries dealing with sensitive health data, and could potentially be applied to similar scenarios in other sectors as well. The way humans perceive and process visual information is significantly influenced by time constraints, affecting their performance in both real-world and laboratory settings. In semi-supervised learning, a significant challenge arises from the disparity in the quality of unlabeled examples.  A common issue is that some examples are noisy, hindering the model's performance.  To address this problem, we propose a novel approach called curriculum learning, which prioritizes and refines the most reliable data first.  Our method, FlexMatch, leverages this principle by first using a strong teacher model to select high-quality examples, and then using a weaker student model to obtain more accurate pseudo labels for less certain examples.  By iteratively applying this process, FlexMatch can effectively improve the performance of the teacher model.  Our extensive experiments demonstrate that FlexMatch outperforms existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art results in image classification tasks, such as ImageNet-1k and ImageNet-22k, as well as in object detection tasks, such as COCO.  The source code for FlexMatch is available on GitHub.  For convenience, we also provide a pre-trained model on the official MMClassification platform. Pretrained multilingual language models, such as multilingual BERT (mBERT), have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in cross-lingual language understanding. This study examines the cross-lingual forecasting performance of mBERT in financial markets, specifically its ability to predict stock prices in languages it has not been trained on. Our results show that mBERT achieves comparable price forecasting accuracy when transferred to new languages, despite not having been directly trained on these languages. Notably, mBERT's performance in languages with limited training data, such as Spanish and Arabic, is particularly strong. To better understand how mBERT achieves this cross-lingual performance, we conducted a series of experiments. Our findings suggest that mBERT's ability to forecast cross-lingual financial data stems from its ability to align its internal representations with those of individual language BERT models, rather than directly encoding language-specific information. This alignment process is facilitated by mBERT's shared vocabulary across languages, allowing it to leverage language agnostic information to make accurate cross-lingual predictions. Overall, our study highlights the remarkable cross-lingual forecasting abilities of mBERT, while also shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that drive its performance. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of effective language models, which, although capable of generating text, struggle with coherent long-term understanding. To address this limitation, we introduce LATTE, a novel Language Trajectory Transformer that leverages its inherent ability to retain long-term context to generate coherent text sequences. By integrating a custom attention mechanism, LATTE is able to track the progression of its text generation trajectory, thus ensuring a consistent and coherent final output. Our experiments demonstrate that LATTE outperforms current state-of-the-art language models in various English text generation tasks, including those involving open-ended and constrained scenarios. Furthermore, we observe that LATTE's ability to retain long-term context is crucial, as its performance degrades significantly when this critical component is omitted. Collaborative filtering methods, widely used in recommender systems, have been enhanced by the incorporation of semi-supervised learning techniques. These semi-supervised approaches, such as the Contrastive and Triangular Contrastive, leverage a two-part training objective consisting of a supervised and an unsupervised component. However, the current implementation of these methods may lead to biased results, as the two components are weighted equally despite the differing importance of their associated biases. To address this limitation, a new, bias-aware margin framework has been proposed, which adjusts the margins based on the relative significance of the two training components. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, a set of experiments was conducted on a series of collaborative filtering tasks, including a comprehensive benchmark of 10M ratings. The results show that the proposed bias-aware margin framework outperforms existing methods, achieving notable improvements in recommendation accuracy. Specifically, the results indicate a 2.5% increase in accuracy for the Contrastive method and a 3.5% improvement for the Triangular Contrastive method, both in terms of Precision@K. Additionally, the proposed framework has been found to be robust and efficient, as it can handle large-scale datasets with millions of users and items. In this paper, we introduce version-driven reclamation, an innovative approach to secure memory safety through a novel runtime mechanism. This method employs a unique data structure that stores memory object information, including version numbers, to track modifications. Our research demonstrates that a single, atomic memory update can efficiently reclaim multiple objects, making it an optimal choice for scenarios involving frequent object modifications. Our design also leverages a global object table to facilitate memory deallocation and incorporates a version-checking mechanism to prevent data access safety breaches. Furthermore, we have developed a compiler-based framework to automatically integrate version-driven reclamation into user programs, thus ensuring memory safety. Additionally, we have successfully integrated version-driven reclamation into the Linux kernel, with our implementation demonstrating superior performance over the existing Ransom's method. By integrating image restoration and region identification in a unified framework, the proposed method effectively enhances both image quality and region accuracy. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world images demonstrate the superiority of this two-stage approach compared to existing state-of-the-art image restoration methods. This approach enables the model to learn more accurately and efficiently. Our proposed method, Enhanced RAMEN, is evaluated on three benchmark datasets and achieves state-of-the-art performance in two of the three datasets. The growing interest in Arabizi, a language model characterized by its reliance on phonetics, has led to an increase in research on the automatic generation of Arabizi transcripts from spoken Arabic. However, existing research has primarily focused on a single task: translating spoken Arabic to Arabizi, ignoring the potential benefits of multi-task learning. In this research, we explore the use of multi-task learning to simultaneously predict multiple levels of Arabizi annotation, including phonemes, syllables, and words. Our approach involves the development of a multi-task sequence forecasting model that can predict all three annotation levels, with the goal of improving the accuracy of each individual prediction. The effectiveness of our model is evaluated using a large, publicly available dataset of spoken Arabic transcriptions. Our results show that the multi-task model outperforms the single-task models in predicting all three annotation levels, with the greatest improvements seen in the prediction of syllables and phonemes. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the three annotation levels and identify areas for future research. Our model and dataset will be made available for public use. Furthermore, we provide insights into the linguistic properties of the Arabizi language, including the distribution of phonemes and syllables. Our research demonstrates that multi-task learning can be an effective approach for improving the accuracy of Arabizi annotation, with potential applications in speech recognition and machine translation. As such, we believe that our work has the potential to inspire new research on the automatic generation of Arabizi transcripts. This study investigates the representation of Uralic languages in low-dimensional space, 
focusing on how well language models capture language-specific characteristics and 
inter-language differences. We utilize two language model types - word embeddings and 
sentence encodings - and evaluate their performance using a range of typological 
characteristics. Our results demonstrate that language models primarily encode 
language-specific characteristics more accurately than universal patterns and 
reveal that different model types are effective depending on the typological feature. 
We also discover that Uralic languages are distinct from Indo-European languages in 
sentence encodings but less distinct in word encodings. Our analysis suggests that 
sentence encodings are effective for morphological and syntactical features, while 
word embeddings are better suited for lexical features. Ultimately, this study reveals 
that language models can be leveraged to analyze and differentiate languages based on 
their unique characteristics. Our code and trained model are available for public use.

Spiking neural networks have gained significant attention due to their potential to mimic biological neural networks and low power consumption. To overcome this, researchers have developed surrogate gradient algorithms, which can be trained using backpropagation. The proposed method is tested on various complex tasks, demonstrating its ability to achieve higher accuracy and better generalization.  The results also highlight the effectiveness of the proposed approach in reducing gradient instability and improving overall performance of surrogate gradient-based SNNs. Our framework involves two key components: first, we segment ads into distinct categories based on their relevance to the user's search; second, we develop a dynamic pricing mechanism that ensures the auction house achieves the highest possible revenue. By combining these components, we create a comprehensive pricing framework that boosts the auction house's revenue without increasing the costs for advertisers. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on a large dataset from Lazada, a prominent e-commerce platform, and found that our proposed framework increases the auction house's revenue by up to 13.9% compared to the traditional method. This study tackles the challenge of estimating a distribution that combines multiple distributions.
The target distribution is represented as a weighted average of individual distributions,
where each weight corresponds to a specific data point subset.
We address the challenge of simultaneously estimating both the target distribution and
the underlying distributions for each subset.

This data is analyzed using a generalized linear mixed model, showcasing the algorithm's utility in determining the shape of the mixing distribution. Additionally, we show how the notion of partial uniform ellipticity can be leveraged to establish the solvability of Dirichlet problems for differential forms. Real-world datasets often contain imbalanced class distributions, where some classes significantly outnumber others. This imbalance issue complicates deep learning model training and testing. While deep learning has seen significant advancements, addressing dataset imbalance remains a pressing concern. In this study, we investigate the impact of imbalanced datasets on self-supervised learning (SSL) and find that these methods exhibit greater robustness compared to supervised learning (SL) when dealing with class imbalance. We examine the performance of prominent SSL models, including SimCLR, MoCo, and BYOL, on imbalanced datasets and compare them to a reweighted SSL model that adapts to changing class distributions. Our results show that these methods achieve comparable performance to traditional SSL on imbalanced datasets. Furthermore, we observe that reweighting SSL can enhance model robustness against imbalanced data. We also explore the effect of imbalanced data on pre-training and fine-tuning, highlighting the potential of SSL-based pre-training to improve downstream task performance. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of SSL in handling imbalanced datasets and open up new avenues for research in this area. Code and data used in this study are publicly available on GitHub. The goal of salient object detection is to pinpoint the most visually prominent objects within images for further analysis. However, the existing methods heavily rely on costly, pixel-level annotations that can be extremely time-consuming and labor-intensive to obtain. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel weakly-supervised approach that leverages minimal annotation, specifically class-level labels, to train a more efficient model. By doing so, the model can effectively identify the most salient pixels within images without the need for extensive, pixel-level supervision. Our approach is grounded in the concept of subitizing, a cognitive phenomenon that describes the rapid identification of small numbers within a scene. In this context, the task of identifying salient objects can be framed as a subitizing problem, where the model learns to pinpoint the most prominent objects within each scene. To achieve this goal, we develop a two-stage training strategy that first trains a scene-level classifier to identify the most prominent objects within each scene, and then refines the model by focusing on the most salient pixels within each image. Our approach is evaluated on five benchmark datasets and outperforms existing weakly-supervised methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying the most salient objects within images. The objective of open-set identification is to determine when a sample does not belong to a known class. This task is crucial for ensuring safety in real-world applications, where misclassifying an unknown sample could have severe consequences. Existing methods for open-set identification are often based on the generalized zero-shot learning approach, which relies on a separate detector trained to recognize out-of-class data. However, these methods have significant drawbacks, including the need for a separate training process and the risk of overfitting. This paper presents an innovative approach to open-set identification that utilizes a single classification model to identify unknown samples. This approach leverages a novel similarity metric, which is trained jointly with the classification model using a modified loss function. This loss function enables the model to learn the distribution of in-class data while accurately distinguishing it from out-of-class data. By integrating a classification model with a similarity metric, this approach eliminates the need for a separate detector, thus enhancing its adaptability and reducing the risk of overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, which outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and ease of implementation. This approach is also highly versatile, allowing it to be easily adapted for use in other applications, such as anomaly detection and unsupervised domain adaptation. High-dimensional time series often exhibit strong interdependencies among their components, which can be effectively modelled using factor models. These factor models can be further refined with additional parameterization, such as in vector autoregressive models that account for both factor and idiosyncratic errors. The introduction of these additional parameters allows for the exploration of temporal relationships between components, which can be particularly useful in clustering-related tasks. Building upon this concept, we propose a clustering method that utilizes factor-adjusted vector autoregressive models to identify distinct patterns in high-dimensional time series data. The proposed approach is demonstrated through its application to stock price analysis, where it is used to segment equity prices in the S&P/TSX composite index during the COVID-19 pandemic. The method's performance is evaluated using simulated data, and it is shown to effectively capture the unique characteristics of each segment. Moreover, an analysis of the factors and idiosyncratic components reveals insights into the underlying drivers of each segment. The results suggest that the proposed method can be a valuable tool for identifying cross-sectional relationships in high-dimensional time series data.
